What does `set -euo pipefail` do at the: `-e` exits the script immediately if any command fails (non-zero exit), instead of silently continuing past an error. `-u` treats referencing an undefined variable as an error rather than silently substituting an empty string, catching typos in variable names. `-o pipefail` makes a pipeline's exit status reflect the first failing command in the pipe, rather than only the last command's status (without it, `false | true` reports success, hiding the real failure) - together these three make a script fail loudly and immediately on the first real problem, instead of continuing to run with corrupted state and failing confusingly later, or not failing at all.
Why does quoting matter in Bash - what's: `$var` unquoted undergoes word-splitting (on whitespace) and glob expansion, so a variable containing spaces or special characters gets split into multiple arguments or has wildcards expanded unexpectedly. `"$var"` (double-quoted) prevents word-splitting and glob expansion while still allowing variable expansion - this is the safe default for referencing a variable. `'$var'` (single-quoted) is a literal string with no expansion at all - the variable name itself is printed, not its value. Forgetting to double-quote a variable that might contain a filename with spaces is one of the most common real-world Bash bugs, causing a command to receive multiple unexpected arguments instead of one.
How would you use `trap` to guarantee cl: `trap 'rm -f "$TMPFILE"' EXIT` registers a cleanup command that runs automatically when the script exits, whether it exits normally, hits an error (with `set -e`), or is interrupted (Ctrl+C sends SIGINT) - this guarantees the cleanup runs in all these cases rather than only on the 'happy path' exit, which is critical for reliably removing temp files, releasing locks, or killing background processes a script started, regardless of how or why the script actually terminates.
What is process substitution in Bash (`<: Process substitution lets a command's output be treated as if it were a file, without writing an actual temp file - `diff <(sort file1) <(sort file2)` runs both sort commands and feeds their output to `diff` as if they were two files, entirely in-memory via a named pipe/file descriptor. This is used whenever a command expects a file argument (not stdin) but you want to feed it the output of another command directly - avoiding the extra step (and cleanup responsibility) of writing intermediate results to disk just to pass them to a command that needs a file path.
What is a heredoc in Bash, and how does: A heredoc (`command <<EOF ... EOF`) feeds a multi-line block of text as input to a command without needing to escape newlines. `<<EOF` (unquoted delimiter) expands variables and command substitutions inside the block normally. `<<'EOF'` (quoted delimiter) treats the entire block as a literal string with no expansion at all - useful when writing a heredoc containing literal `$` characters or backticks you don't want interpreted (e.g. generating a config file template containing shell-like syntax that should be written verbatim, not evaluated).
How does Bash handle exit codes, and wha: Every command sets an exit status (0 for success, non-zero for failure) accessible immediately afterward via `$?` - but `$?` is fragile since it reflects the *last* command run, so any command executed in between (even an unrelated `echo` for debugging) silently overwrites it before you check it. `if command; then ... fi` checks the exit status directly and immediately as part of the control flow, without that fragile intermediate step, which is why idiomatic Bash almost always tests a command's success directly in an `if`/`while` condition rather than running it separately and checking `$?` afterward.
How would you declare and iterate over a: Declare with `arr=(one two three)`, access an element with `${arr[1]}` (zero-indexed), and iterate with `for item in "${arr[@]}"; do ... done`. `"${arr[@]}"` (double-quoted, with @) expands to each element as a separate, correctly-quoted word - the correct choice for iteration since it preserves elements containing spaces as single items. `"${arr[*]}"` expands to all elements joined into a single string (separated by the first character of `$IFS`, space by default) - almost never what you want for iteration, since it collapses the array into one word rather than preserving individual elements.
Explain Bash parameter expansion default: `${VAR:-default}` evaluates to `VAR`'s value if set and non-empty, otherwise to `default`, without modifying `VAR` itself - useful for providing a fallback inline. `${VAR:=default}` does the same but also assigns `default` back into `VAR` if it was unset/empty, so subsequent references to `VAR` see the default too. `${VAR:?error message}` causes the script to exit immediately with the given error message printed if `VAR` is unset/empty - a concise way to enforce that a required variable/argument was actually provided before proceeding, rather than continuing with an empty value and failing confusingly later.
How would you write a cron-scheduled scr: Never assume cron has the same PATH, environment variables, or working directory as an interactive shell - explicitly set `PATH` at the top of the script (or use absolute paths for every command), source any needed environment file explicitly rather than relying on `.bashrc`/`.profile` (cron doesn't load them), and `cd` to an explicit absolute working directory before doing anything relative-path-dependent. Redirect both stdout and stderr to a log file (`>> /var/log/myjob.log 2>&1`) since cron's own error emails are easy to miss or misconfigured, and this is by far the most common category of 'works when I run it manually, fails silently under cron' bug.
How would you debug a Bash script that's: `set -x` (or running the script with `bash -x script.sh`) prints every command to stderr immediately before executing it, with variables already expanded - showing exactly what actually ran, not just what's written in the source, which surfaces issues like an unexpectedly empty variable or a glob expanding differently than intended. To debug just one section rather than the whole script, wrap only that section with `set -x` before it and `set +x` immediately after, avoiding a wall of noisy trace output for parts of the script you already know work correctly.
What is the difference between running a: `./script.sh` (with execute permission set) runs the script using whatever interpreter is specified in its shebang line (`#!/bin/bash` or `#!/bin/sh`), which is why the shebang matters - it's the authoritative declaration of which shell should interpret the script. Explicitly running `sh script.sh` or `bash script.sh` overrides the shebang and forces that specific interpreter regardless of what's declared - this matters because `sh` on many systems is actually `dash` (a POSIX-compliant but more limited shell) rather than bash, so a script using bash-specific features (arrays, `[[ ]]`) will fail or behave differently if accidentally run with `sh` instead of the bash it was actually written for.
When would you use `xargs` instead of a: `xargs` is preferred when you want to batch multiple items into fewer invocations of a command (e.g. passing many filenames to `rm` in one call instead of one `rm` call per file in a loop, which is significantly faster for large lists) or when you need to parallelize with `-P`. The common pitfall: `xargs` by default splits input on whitespace, so filenames containing spaces get incorrectly split into multiple arguments - the fix is using null-delimited input throughout the pipeline (`find . -print0 | xargs -0 command`), which uses the null byte as a delimiter since it can never legally appear in a filename, unlike whitespace.
What are common string manipulation tech: Bash's built-in parameter expansion handles simple cases without spawning an external process - `${var#prefix}`/`${var%suffix}` strip a prefix/suffix, `${var/old/new}` does a single substitution, `${var//old/new}` replaces all occurrences, and `${var:0:5}` extracts a substring - these are fast since they avoid forking a subprocess. Reach for `sed`/`awk` when the manipulation needs actual pattern matching (regex), operates across multiple lines/fields in structured text, or needs to process input from a file/pipe rather than a single variable already in memory - using `sed` for a simple single-variable string replace that parameter expansion could handle is unnecessary overhead, but trying to force complex multi-line text processing into parameter expansion alone is fighting the wrong tool.
How would you write automated tests for: Bats lets you write test cases in a familiar `@test "description" { ... }` structure, asserting on a command's exit status and output (stdout/stderr) programmatically, and integrates with CI the same way any other test suite does - giving automated, repeatable verification instead of manually running a script and eyeballing whether the output looks right. This matters especially for scripts with conditional logic or error-handling paths (a disk-full scenario, a missing argument) that are impractical to manually re-verify by hand on every change, but are straightforward to encode as automated Bats test cases run on every commit.
